description: Geo Anvesha is a student team using Earth observation, geospatial technology, and thoughtful software design to understand how Earth changes. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are exploring Dancing with the SARs and NISAR radar data to study flooding, ground movement, agricultural change, and other surface processes. We aim to build a useful and scientifically honest solution for disaster response.
summary:
Terra Sutra turns complex satellite data into a clear picture of how our planet is changing. It brings together regional observations, interactive maps, timelines and understandable explanations to help people explore environmental change.

The project covers flooding in the Brahmaputra floodplains and Chennai coastal plain, glacier change at Pine Island Glacier, forest fires across India, soil moisture in Moga, and ground movement in Mexico City. Each module connects a specific environmental question to relevant data and analytical methods.

Users can search by place and date, compare observations, explore available time-lapse maps and examine charts. Behind these visuals, a shared backend organises measurements, processing outputs and source information, keeping every finding traceable.

Terra Sutra uses historical Sentinel-1 radar observations alongside other relevant datasets, with scope to incorporate suitable NISAR products. A proposed voice-enabled assistant helps users navigate the platform and understand its evidence, while optional field sensors add local environmental context.

Rather than promising to predict every disaster, Terra Sutra makes environmental evidence easier to explore, question and understand. It distinguishes measured observations from possible interpretations, helping users see both what the data reveals and where uncertainty remains.
details:
Terra Sutra: Making Earth’s Changes Understandable

Terra Sutra is an environmental-change exploration project that brings regional satellite analyses into a shared, accessible interface. It connects maps, charts, observation dates and plain-language explanations so users can understand not just what appears to have changed, but what the measurements mean and where uncertainty remains.

What it does and how it works

Our regional studies cover Brahmaputra floodplains, Pine Island Glacier, forest fires across India, soil moisture in Moga, Mexico City ground displacement and Chennai coastal-plain flooding.

Each module addresses a distinct question. Flood analysis examines candidate inundation; glacier analysis considers ice-surface change and crevasse context; fire observations identify thermal detections; soil-moisture products describe water content; and displacement analysis screens possible ground movement.

The analytical workflow connects a defined geographical area and observation period with source data, quality checks, processing methods and visual outputs. The platform design supports searches by place and date, comparisons between observations, and temporal playback where multiple dated maps exist. Missing observations remain gaps rather than being replaced with invented frames.

The project uses historical Sentinel-1 radar observations and relevant supporting datasets. Sentinel-1 and NISAR are different missions: our historical analyses are not presented as NISAR observations. The architecture can accommodate suitable NISAR products as their coverage and processing requirements are established.

Benefits and intended impact

Environmental datasets are often difficult to access and interpret without specialist knowledge. Terra Sutra aims to reduce that barrier for students, researchers and public audiences by keeping measurements, visualisations and explanations together.

Its intended impact is better-informed environmental understanding—not guaranteed disaster prediction. Source attribution, observation dates, units and limitations help users distinguish measured change from a possible interpretation.

Tools, software and development approach

The supplied Brahmaputra module uses Sentinel-1 radar observations, water-change classification and land-cover comparison. The Mexico City module uses NASA OPERA Sentinel-1 displacement products, quality filtering and connected-group screening, with outputs including geographic polygons, tables and visualisations.

The broader platform’s technical design uses Python for processing and analysis, CSV tables for structured outputs, and geographically referenced rasters and map files. The proposed shared application uses PostgreSQL with PostGIS for spatial records, a backend interface for retrieving results, and React with an interactive mapping library for the website.

A proposed language-model assistant retrieves approved records and explains them rather than inventing measurements. Voice input and spoken responses extend this interaction. An optional ESP32-based environmental node adds local temperature, humidity, pressure and soil-wetness context. These platform and hardware components are design elements unless demonstrated in the submitted implementation.

Creativity and team considerations

Terra Sutra’s creative contribution is connecting different environmental questions through one evidence-centred experience while preserving their scientific differences. A flood candidate, thermal detection and displacement measurement are not treated as interchangeable hazard scores.

Our team considered regional relevance, historical coverage, storage requirements, reproducibility, accessibility and uncertainty. We also considered differences in spatial resolution, acquisition timing and measurement quality. These choices support a project that is understandable and visually engaging without overstating what its data can prove.
